images.filename: The Metropolitan (Lincoln First Bank Building), Clinton Avenue, Rochester, NY (54420831839).jpg
images.caption: Built in 1973, this Modern International-style building was designed by John Graham and Company for Lincoln First Bank to serve as the company’s headquarters and a commercial office building.  The building stands 27 stories and 392 feet (119 meters) tall, and is the third-tallest building in the city of Rochester.  The building is distinctive for its vertical fins, clad in white metal panels, which taper outwards with the building’s form towards the base, while the rest of the exterior is clad in a dark curtain wall with black spandrels and mullions, giving the building an extremely sleek, minimalist appearance.  The building is a contributing structure in the East Main Street Historic District, listed on the National Register of Historic Places in 2017.   Today, the building continues to serve as a commercial office building, now known as The Metropolitan.

images.filename: View from Broad Street Bridge, Rochester, NY (54421020160).jpg
images.caption: Founded in 1788, the city of Rochester grew rapidly following the arrival of the Erie Canal in 1823, with the city’s location around the falls of the Genesee River providing abundant power for industrial operations, leading to it being incorporated as a city in 1834.  The city served as a major wheat processing center during the mid-19th Century, as well as being home to a significant plant nursery industry, and later became the home of significant companies, including Western Union, Xerox, Bausch and Lomb, and Eastman Kodak.  The city was also a significant site for various civil rights movements, including being the home of Frederick Douglass and Susan B. Anthony, and is situated near where the 1848 Seneca Falls convention, largely seen as the origin of the women’s suffrage movement in the United States.  The city developed a major garment industry in the early 20th Century, but the city’s population began to decline after World War II, due to similar trends seen in other cities, including white flight, suburbanization, and the relocation of industry and jobs.  The city today sits at the center of a metropolitan area with a population of approximately 1 million people, and is home to several cultural institutions, museums, and a revitalized downtown core.

images.caption: The facade of the Eastman Theatre, an historic auditorium in Rochester, New York.  Conceived by, and named for, photography pioneer and philanthropist George Eastman, the Theatre opened in 1922.  This is the primary performance space for the large ensembles at the Eastman School of Music and for the Rochester Philharmonic Orchestra.  The streets in the foreground are East Main Street (left) and Gibbs Street (right).

images.caption:
The Geva Theatre Center in Rochester, New York.  This building, which was added to the National Register of Historic Places in 1985, was originally constructed in 1868 as a Naval Armory and Convention Hall.  It was renovated to house two theaters in 1972.  This photograph, with the camera facing northwest, shows the rear of the building, with the NextStage entrance.  The main entrance is on the north side of the building.

New York State Route 15 northbound runs along the one-way street South Clinton Avenue in the foreground, terminating at the intersection with Woodbury Boulevard on the right edge of the image.  Woodbury Boulevard here carries New York State Route 31 eastbound (left to right).

images.caption: The Charlotte-Genesee Lighthouse in Charlotte, the northernmost neighborhood of Rochester, New York.  Built in 1822, the light tower is 40 feet tall.  It was deactivated in 1881.  It was saved from destruction in 1965 and is now a museum operated by a nonprofit agency for Monroe County.  It is listed on the National Register of Historic Places.
